div.p: Over the last few decades geo-and thermochronological techniques based on the accumulation of radiogenic 4 He in minerals have gained popularity. Currently there is no mineral-based 4 He reference material that allows routine screening of gas extraction and measurement procedures. The commonly-used mineral reference material for (U-Th)/He thermochronology have variable U and Th contents which result in variable 4 He concentrations. Here we demonstrate that native platinum grains (RS-Pt) from placer deposits in the Santiago River, Ecuador, yield constant 4 He contents and may be used as a reference material. Helium concentrations measured at the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre (n = 8) and Institute of Precambrian Geology and Geochronology RAS (n = 9) noble gas laboratories yield mean 4 He concentrations that overlap at the 95% confidence level. The weighted mean 4 He concentration is 215 ± 2 × 10 11 at g -1 (2s) and mean 190 Pt-4 He age is 39.6 ± 0.7 Ma (2s). Geo-and thermochronological techniques based on radiogenic helium accumulation in minerals have gained increasing prominence in the last 20 years or so. (U-Th)/He ages of apatites are now widely exploited for low temperature thermochronology (e.g., Farley et al. 2002). The technique is now routinely applied to several other minerals and has found a wide range of applications in geoscience (e.g., Flowers et al. 2022). Helium dating of iron oxyhydroxide phases is used to determine the age and duration of weathering processes (e.g., Shuster et al. 2005) and when applied to ore minerals provides constraints on the timing of mineralisation (e.g., Shukolyukov et al. 2012, Wu et al. 2019, Yakubovich et al. 2020, Benites et al. 2022). The technique can be used for dating young volcanic eruptions (Danisik et al. 2012) and the age of groundwaters can be reconstructed based on 4 He concentrations in quartz (Tolstikhin et al. 2005).

Mineral reference materials are essential for accurate measurements as well as monitoring of instrument performance as they replicate the most important aspects of the measurement procedure. Conventionally mass spectrometers used for He isotope measurements are calibrated using standard gases such as HESJ (Matsuda et al. 2002) or air (Oliver et al. 1984).

Using gas calibration materials to determine instrument sensitivity requires precise knowledge of the reservoir and pipette volumes and He pressure in the reservoir. The failure of pipettes can be difficult to detect leaving gas reservoirs depleted. Mineral He abundance reference materials, such as the CRONUS-P pyroxene for cosmogenic 3 He (Blard et al. 2015), have been distributed internationally and provide a way of tracking the efficiency of gas extraction as well as mass spectrometer performance. Several mineral age reference materials for apatite and zircon (U-Th)/He dating are now widely distributed. They require additional measurements of U and Th (and Sm) mass fractions. Inherent variability in the U and Th mass fraction at the sample size typically used mean they cannot be used for determining He measurement procedures alone (Boyce andHodges 2001, Dobson et al. 2008). Geological reference materials, such as the Columbia River basalt, USGS BCR-2 (Ferreira et al. 1975) and the Knyahinya meteorite (Shultz and Franke 2004), have been developed as 4 He reference material but were never widely used. Natural Pt-alloy grains have potential as 4 He reference material because (i) the alpha particle-producing isotope ( 190 Pt) is homogeneously distributed within the mineral, which implies homogeneous distribution of the daughter 4 He (Shukolyukov et al. 2011); (ii) 4 He is not lost by diffusion from Pt-alloys at temperatures below 900 °C (Shukolyukov et al. 2012a, b); (iii) abrasive removal of grain rims during transport means recoil loss of He from the detrital grains is negligible, and (iv) the range of He concentrations in the native Pt-alloys (10 -4 -10 -7 cm 3 STP g -1 ; Shukolyukov et al. 2012b) mean single grains can supply 4 He amounts that are in the range commonly measured in natural samples.

Given the recent increase in the number of laboratories making He measurements there is a pressing need for reference material that can be used quickly to test the veracity of gas extraction techniques and accuracy of mass spectrometer calibration. Here we report 4 He mass fraction (concentration) and gas content and 190 Pt-4 He age of detrital native platinum grains from the medial reach placer deposit of the Santiago River, Ecuador, and assess their potential as a reference material.

div.head: Platinum placer deposits
div.p: Millimetre size grains of Pt-alloys are rarely found in bedrock but they are abundant in many alluvial placer deposits. For instance, approximately 370 tonnes of platinum have been mined from the placers associated with the Ural Platiniferous Belt (Stepanov et al. 2019), 120 tones from the Kondyor-Uorgalan placer deposit, Aldan shield, Russia (Mochalov 2019), and 25 tonnes from Goodnews Bay in Alaska (Barker and Lamal 1988).

Dunite-clinopyroxenite Ural-Alaskan-and alkaline ultramafic Aldan-type complexes are the predominant source of platinum-group minerals (PGM) in alluvial deposits worldwide (Cabri et al. 2022). According to the IMA classification, Pt-alloy grains with ≥ 80 at.% Pt are considered to be native platinum, while grains with bulk compositions that are close to Pt3Fe, albeit without strict composition limits, are termed isoferroplatinum (Cabri and Feather, 1975). The dominant PGM in placer deposits are Pt-Fe alloys, particularly isoferroplatinum (Pt3Fe) (Mochalov et al. 2013) PGM are extracted from ultramafic rocks by weathering and mechanically transported in fluvial systems that can last for millions of years (Yakubovich et al. 2019). During transportation Pt-alloy grains mechanically deform, which may result in change of Pt3Fe crystal lattice from primitive cubic Pm-3m to face-centred Fm-3m cell (Mochalov et al. 2018). There is no evidence of a newly formation of Pt-alloys in a placer deposits (Cabri et al. 2022).

div.head: Helium in Pt-alloy grains
div.p: The main source of radiogenic 4 He in Pt-alloys is the α-decay of 190 Pt (Shukolyukov et al. 2012b). 190 Pt- 4 He ages (t) can be calculated using determinations of the He and Pt content of grains using the formula:

div.p: where 𝜆𝜆 190 is the 190 Pt decay constant (1.477 × 10 -12 y -1 , Walker et al. 1997) and 𝑓𝑓 190 is the natural abundance of 190 Pt (0.01296%, Walker et al. 1997). Diffusive loss of He, alpha-recoil, radiation damage, mineral impurities, recrystallisation, and fluid inclusions can affect mineral He ages (Flowers et al. 2022).

The thermal retentivity of 4 He in Pt-alloys is high. Numerous studies have shown that He has an extremely low solubility in metals at least at temperatures below half of the melt temperature (0.5 Tm), tending to be trapped by vacancies with the formation of He-V clusters (e.g., Trinkaus and Singh 2003). The high retentivity of He in native metals has been empirically confirmed by diffusion experiments (Shukolyukov et al., 2012a, b) and by the 190 Pt-4 He ages of a wide variety of deposits and ore-occurrences (Okrugin et al. 2020, Berdnikov et al. 2020, Mochalov et al. 2021, Yakubovich et al. 2022a). So far, there is no evidence for the open-system behaviour of the 190 Pt-4 He isotope system (Yakubovich et al. 2022b).

Alpha-recoil loss 190 Pt decay produces only one alpha-particle with a stopping distance of 4.7 μm in isoferroplatinum (Yakubovich et al. 2022a). This implies that less than 2% of the total He Kutyrev et al. 2021), thus less than 0.2% of the 4 He in a 1 mg spherical grain is implanted (Yakubovich et al. 2022a). Transportation of Pt grains in river systems for even short distances leads to the abrasive removal of the grain exterior (Hallbauer andUtter 1977, Shumilov 1981). Thus, for rounded Pt-grains derived from the modern placer deposits alpharecoil corrections are not required.

div.head: Radiation damage
div.p: This affects the rate of He loss from silicate and oxide minerals (Shuster et al. 2006, Yakubovich et al. 2010, Guenthner et al. 2013). Metals do not accumulate radiation damage as nuclear tracks are immediately annealed (Fleischer et al. 1975). Thus, there is no evidence that self-radiation of Pt-alloys results in enhanced He loss from grains.

div.head: Impurities
div.p: Incorporation of U and Th in Pt-alloys can be an additional source of 4 He. The mass fraction of U and Th in PGMs typically does not exceed 50 ng g -1 and 25 ng g -1 , respectively (Yakubovich 2013, Cabral et al. 2022) and do not affect 190 Pt-4 He ages (Shukolyukov et al. 2012b).

div.head: Recrystallisation
div.p: Platinum-alloys are chemically inert and robust (Cabri et al. 2022) which prevents He and Pt loss during weathering and transport. 190 Pt-4 He ages of Pt-Fe alloy grains from lode deposits have been shown to be identical to those from corresponding alluvial placers (Mochalov et al. 2018). Extensive mechanical deformation which cause structural transformation of the Ptalloys does not appear to induce 4 He loss, although there is evidence of redistribution of the defects within the crystal structure which result in slight variability of 4 He concentrations in a various fragment of the deformed grain (Mochalov et al. 2018).

div.head: Fluid inclusions
div.p: The concentration of fluid-derived He in minerals formed in magmatic and hydrothermal processes typically does not exceed 10 -8 cm 3 STP g -1 (Stuart et al. 1994, Graupner et al. 2006). This is less than 1% of the He in Mesozoic and older Pt-grains (see fig. 1 in Shukolyukov et al. 2012b). In rare cases the concentration of trapped He in Pt-alloys might

div.head: Mineralogical description
div.p: Grains selected from RS-1 concentrate (n = 113) were studied under the electron microscope.

The chemical composition of sixty-three grains was determined. Platinum mass fractions vary The Pt-alloys are compositionally homogeneous, no chemically distinct rims or secondary mineral phases were observed (Figure 5). Mineral inclusions were observed in only three grains of native platinum. In one case an inclusion of amphibole was observed (30 µm × 40 µm) (Figure 6a). Others are represented by small (30-50 µm) inclusions of tetraauricupride (AuCu) with chalcopyrite (Figure 6b). Native platinum makes up more than 85% of all PGM grains, in other cases isoferroplatinum occurs.
Platinum grains are rounded (Figure 5). The surfaces typically have cracks which common for the grains derived from placer deposits (Figure 7).

div.head: Helium measurement results
div.p: Eight grains of native platinum (RS-Pt) were analysed at SUERC and nine grains at IPGG RAS (Table 1). The full chemical composition data is available for two grains measured in SUERC (7, 8) and for six grains measured in IPGG RAS (9,(11)(12)(13)(14)17) in Table 2. The grains ranged in mass from 0.645 to 3.359 mg. 4 He concentrations vary from 1.99 to 2.22 × 10 13 at g -1 . The 4 He concentration of grains measured at SUERC show a slightly higher intermediate precision (1.6%, MSWD = 1.3) than the measurements done at IPGG RAS (2.9%, MSWD = 0.8) (Table 1, Figure 8). The weighted mean 4 He concentration measured at SUERC (215 ± 2 × 10 11 at g -1 , 2s) and IPGG RAS (211 ± 5 × 10 11 at g -1 , 2s) overlap at the 95% confidence level. The weighted mean 4 He concentration for all data 215 ± 2 × 10 11 at g - 1 . 3 He never exceeded 3 × 10 4 at, which is a hot blank level of the Helix SFT massspectrometer in SUERC.

190 Pt-4 He age calculations 190 Pt-4 He ages were calculated only for the grains for which Pt mass fraction and He gas content was directly measured, in total eight grains. The weighted mean 190 Pt-4 He age is 39.6 ± 0.7 Ma (2s) (Table 2). The intermediate precision of the 190 Pt-4 He ages obtained in IPGG RAS for six samples is 2.6% and is slightly lower than the intermediate precision of the 4 He concentration values (2.9%), which implies that variability in a mass fraction of Pt in the grains affect the 4 He content.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: the San Juan Formation. It consists of dunites, layered wehrlites, gabbros and amphibole gabbros, and has been dated at 87.1 ± 1.7 Ma by zircon U-Pb (Vallejo 2007) and 99.2 ± 1.3
Ma by 40 Ar/ 39 Ar of amphiboles (Mamberti et al. 2004).
The geology of the Western Cordillera during Middle to Late Eocene times is characterised by the existence of a volcanic arc. The more widespread formation is the so-called Macuchi

Unit that is mainly composed of basalts and basaltic andesites, which were erupted at 42.6 ± 1.3 Ma (Vallejo 2007). The Rio Santiago Placer deposit must be derived from an Eocene Ural-Alaskan-type complex hidden somewhere in the Western Cordillera. The absence of measurable 3 He in the Pt-alloy grains from the Santiago River indicates rapid erosion and minimal surface residence; the concentration of cosmogenic 3 He in the metal grains from the alluvium deposits is typically higher (Yakubovich et al. 2019).

div.head: Possibility of inter-laboratory cross calibration
div.p: The number of laboratories that use He isotope measurements for geochronology and geochemistry is increasing and there are currently significant efforts being undertaken to systematise protocols for reporting (U-Th)/He data (Flowers et al. 2022). There is no widely available reference material for determining the laboratory relative bias of 4 He measurement results. The RS-Pt grains can be used by individual laboratories as a rapid test of instrument sensitivity and more broadly it has potential to as an inter-laboratory calibration tool.

The application of the RS-Pt grains as He reference material requires measurement of Pt mass fraction. Native platinum makes up ~ 85% of the Pt-alloys of the RS-Pt concentrate, and it is hard to separate it visually from other Pt-alloys. Thus, for calibration purposes grains should be studied using electron microscopy (see Methods section). For inter-laboratory cross calibration studies Pt mass fraction of the RS-Pt grains can be made at the IPGG RAS laboratory (contact olya.v.yakubovich@gmail.com). Samples of the Pt concentrate are available on request from the SUERC Noble Gas laboratory (contact fin.stuart@glasgow.ac.uk). a Grain 1 was excluded from the calculation as it does not overlap within 99% confidence with weighted mean value obtained for other seven grains measured in SUERC, thus it can be considered as an erroneous measurement result.

Fluid derived4 He release from Pt-alloys at temperatures below 1000 °C, when the in situ radiogenic4 He requires melting of the metal(Yakubovich 2013, Cabral et al. 2022). Typically, the amount of low temperature4 He is insignificant and does not exceed the first few percent of the total 4 He budget. Platinumalloys associated with Ural-Alaskan-type complexes appear to have negligible trapped4 He(Yakubovich 2013).Mineral inclusionsPlatinum-alloy grains commonly contain PGE-bearing (native iridium, osmium, laurite etc.) and silicate (chromite, olivine, clinopyroxene) mineral inclusions (e.g., fig.4inGervilla et al. 2020). Late hydrothermal alteration might result in the formation of rims of Fe-and Cu-rich tetragonal Pt-Fe alloys, such as tetraferroplatinum, tulameenite. These might affect 190 Pt-4 He ages. Platinum-alloys are not transparent which excludes optical methods for determining the presence of mineral inclusions. The capability of microtomography is limited for the dense mm-size Pt-Fe grains, as darkening occurs in the centre part of the grains (200-300 μm) due to the insufficient radiation power(Okrugin et al. 2020). Thus, grains used for 190 Pt-4 He dating should be studied under electron microscope in polished mounts for phase homogeneity, presence of the inclusions and Pt concentration prior to4 He measurement.

gold placers in the Santiago River, Esmeraldas Province in the Ecuadorian Western Cordillera occur in alluvial terraces consisting of ~ 5 m thick gravels that overlie marine sediments of the Onzole and Bordón Formations(López-Males et al. 2020). The auriferous gravels evolve upwards to more sandy units (up to 5 m) that have lower Au contents. These are topped by barren layers (0.30-1 m) of sand, gravel and mainly clays. Although no data are available on the bulk-rock Au contents, a heavy mineral concentrate from the auriferous gravels mainly composed of ilmenite with some quartz and magnetite, revealed up to 17.3 µg g -1 Au and 27.5 µg g -1 PGE (López-Males et al. 2020). The gold is concentrated by amalgamation by the local miners, while the platinum nuggets are usually discarded. We have acquired a ~ 300 g platinum-rich concentrate (RS-1) that contains a few hundred Ptbearing grains (Figure1). The sample was collected in the medial reach of the Santiago River: E736800, N10103380, 55 m above sea level. Coordinates reference system is

SIRGAS2000 that corresponds with an UTM projection in the zone 17S and a datum "World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS84)". Platinum grains are typically rounded and flat, grain diameters varying from 200 to 1800 µm and mass 0.1-10 mg.The PGMs are dominated by native platinum (91% m/m Pt) with minor isoferroplatinum(Weiser and Schmidt-Thom 1993, Gervilla et al. 2020, López-Males et al. 2020). Based on the PGM mineralogy (Pt-Fe alloy, tulameenite, hongshiite, cuprorhodsite, cooperate, bowieite, erlichmanite, laurite, braggite, sperrylite osmium and unnamed (Pt,Pd)3(As,Sb,Te)Pt12Cu8S5 phase),Weiser and Schmidt-Thome (1993) andLópez-Males et al. (2020) have proposed that the grains originate from an Ural-Alaskan-type maficultramafic intrusion. However, the nature and location of the source rock are unknown.Measurement proceduresMeasurement of Pt mass fractionIndividual Pt grains were mounted and polished for electron microscopy. Chemical analysis of the grains was conducted using JSM-6510LA scanning electron microscope with JED-2200 EDS add-on at the Institute of Precambrian Geology and Geochronology RAS, St.Petersburg. Pure metals were used as calibration materials for PGE (Pt, Os, Ir, Ru, Rh, Pd), Ni and Fe; CuFeS2 for Cu. The measurement conditions were accelerating voltage 20 kV, current 1.5 nA. The following X-ray lines were used: Mα for Pt, Os, Ir; Lα for Ru, Rh, Pd; Kα for Fe, Ni and Cu. Th detection limit for PGE is 0.01% m/m. The combined standard uncertainty of Pt determinations estimated based on the deviation of the sum of all mass fractions from 100% and the instrument intermediate precision by summation in quadrature, according to the suggestions in EURACHEM/CITAC Guide (2012).Platinum-alloy grains that yielded chemical composition of native platinum (~ 91% m/m Pt; RS-Pt) without visible inclusions were retrieved from the mounts and washed in acetone in an ultrasonic cleaner for 15 min and weighed on a micro-balance (resolution 0.001 mg) prior to He measurement. Repeated measurements of the same grains in the same beaker revealed that the standard uncertainty of the mass measurement procedure is 0.003 mg.Helium measurementsHelium concentrations in native platinum (RS-Pt) have been measured in two laboratories with different measurement principles. At the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre (SUERC) Noble Gas Laboratory helium was extracted by directly heating single Pt grains with a focused beam of an 808 nm diode laser(Stuart et al. 1999). Grains were loaded into individual recesses in a Cu pan. Platinum foil was used to determine a representative hot blank. All samples were heated at 75-95% of the laser power for 5-10 min. During heating the Pt-grains melt to a ball which requires 1700-1800 °C. The mean4 He hot blanks in the experiments with Pt foil was 7 × 10 8 atoms. A video of Pt-melting by a diode laser in the SUERC laboratory is available in the online supporting information (Video S1). The amount of He released was determined using a ThermoFisher Helix-SFT magnetic sector mass spectrometer(Carracedo et al. 2019).4 He + signal intensity expressed in fA was measured on the Faraday cup, while the 3 He signal (fA) was simultaneously measured on the Secondary Electron Multiplier. Mass spectrometer sensitivity was determined by repeated measurements of aliquots of He from a reservoir of the HESJ standard(Matsuda et al. 2002). The combined standard uncertainty of each of He measurement result was calculated by summation in quadrature of (i) the repeatability precision of twenty readings of4 He revealed from the deviation of the measurement results from the ion depletion line using the Qtegra software (Thermo Fischer Scientific); (ii) intermediate precision of the hot blank measurement results;(iii) and the uncertainty component derived from the calibration of the mass-spectrometer by HESJ gas standard.Helium gas content measurements in the Institute of Precambrian Geology and Geochronology (IPGG) RAS was performed using the high-sensitivity magnetic sector mass spectrometer MSU-G-01-M equipped with a high-vacuum furnace (Spectron-Analyt, Saint-Petersburg;Shukolyukov et al. 2012a, b). A Secondary Electron Multiplier was used for determination of the 4 He + beam intensity (cps). Calibration of the mass spectrometer was done using the Knyahinya meteorite reference material (1.24 ± 0.02 10 -5 cm 3 STP g -1 of 4 He,Schultz and Franke 2004). The furnace cannot produce temperatures that are required for melting of pure Pt (1700-1800 °C) so the Pt grains were mixed with annealed Cu wire (99.95% purity) in the mass ratio 1:3 and wrapped in Ta foil. The Cu reduces the melting temperature of the Pt-alloy to approximately 1400 °C(Shukolyukov et al. 2012b). Heating was done in rhenium cuvette in several steps. A long (30 min) preheating at 800 °C was followed by 15 min at 1450 °C. Temperature calibration was done using a thermocouple connected to the Re cuvette. Tantalum foil with Cu wire was used to determine a representative hot blank level. The average 4 He blank was 3 × 10 9 atoms. The combined standard uncertainty of each of He measurement result was calculated by summation in quadrature of the (i) repeatability precision revealed from ten readings of 4 He; (ii) intermediate precision of the hot blank measurement results; and (iii) the uncertainty component derived from the calibration of the mass-spectrometer by Knyahinya meteorite geological reference material. 190 Pt-4 He dating 190 Pt-4 He ages were calculated based on Equation (1). The combined measurement uncertainty was estimated based on the grain mass, Pt, and He uncertainties from the mass fraction measurement results following the procedure in EURACHEM/CITAC Guide (2012).

The Pt-Fe alloy grains are characterised by low Ru (0.3% m/m) and Os (< 1.2% m/m) contents. Higher mass fractions are typical for Rh (up to 3.4% m/m) and Pd (3.5% m/m). Iridium is rare, but can reach 1.2% m/m (Figure 4). Copper is a common impurity in most grains and can reach 2% m/m when Ni does not exceed 0.4% m/m.

Native platinum alloy grains from the Santiago River, Ecuador, (RS-Pt) have an interlaboratory reproducibility weighted mean4 He concentration of 215 ± 2.0 × 10 11 at g -1 (2s) and190 Pt-4 He age of 39.6 ± 0.7 Ma (2s). Consequently, these grains can be used for calibration and monitoring the performance of He measurement systems. Currently tens of thousands of Pt grains are available, which could cover the calibration needs of He laboratories for years. We recommend that laboratories reporting measurement of4 He concentrations report their own measurement results of4 He mass fraction and 190 Pt-4 He age of RS-Pt grains as well as measurement uncertainties budget in order to eliminate interlaboratory calibration errors.

div.head: Pt-alloys from the Santiago River as a 4 He reference material
div.p: Native platinum (RS-Pt) grains from the Santiago River, Ecuador, yield homogeneous 4 He concentrations with mean of 215 ± 2.0 × 10 11 at g -1 . The repeatability of 4 He content depends on (i) repeatability precision of the 4 He measurement results, and (ii) initial homogeneity of 4 He in the RS-Pt grain.

The repeatability precision of the mass spectrometer He measurement can be determined independently by the repeated measurements of gas aliquots. The repeatability of He gas content of the HESJ reference gas at SUERC (standard deviation 1.15%) is close to that measured in grains (1.6%).

The repeatability precision of the multiplier of the MSU-M-G-01-M mass spectrometer, which is considered as a square root of the signal size (counts per second) was 2-4% during the measurement period. This is in a line with intermediate precision of He content measured at IPGG RAS (2.9%). The deviation of the 4 He content of grains measured at IPGG RAS reflects the repeatability precision of the instrument not heterogeneity of the RS-Pt grains.

If we assume that Pt-alloy grains crystallised instantaneously during rapid cooling during magma emplacement the variation of 4 He concentration in Pt-alloys should reflect the precision of Pt mass fraction. The dispersion of Pt concentration in the native platinum from RS-Pt concentrate is 0.62%. Thus, initial homogeneity of 4 He the RS-Pt is close to that value.

Given that the concentration of 4 He is Pt-dependent the 190 Pt-4 He ages of RS-Pt are more homogenous than 4 He concentrations alone. For instance, 190 Pt-4 He ages at IPGG RAS (2.6%) have better precision than 4 He concentration measurement results (2.9%). That implies that RS-Pt grains can be used both as He and 190 Pt-4 He age reference materials.

div.head: Geological implications
div.p: The 190 Pt-4 He age of the RS-Pt grains is 39.6 ± 0.7 Ma (n = 8). This is older than the Ultramafic Alto Condoto Complex in Colombia (20.7 ± 1 and 19.6 ± 0.15 Ma by K-Ar dating of hornblende; Salinas et al. 1994), which is the only Ural-Alaskan-type complex known in the Andean Cordillera and is likely the source of some placer deposits of the Chocó region.
The 190 Pt-4 He age of the Santiago River platinum is much younger than the only known mineral formations in the Western Cordillera of Ecuador that contain mafic-ultramafic rocks;
